description: Calculate molar concentrations, convert moles and volumes, and solve titration problems.
content_html:
Molar Concentration

Chemists need to know not just what a solution contains but how much. Concentration tells us the amount of solute dissolved per unit volume of solution. The standard unit is mol/dm³ (moles per cubic decimetre, also called moles per litre). The relationship is:

$$\text{concentration (mol/dm}^3\text{)} = \frac{\text{amount of solute (mol)}}{\text{volume of solution (dm}^3\text{)}}$$

Rearranging gives two other useful forms: \(n = c \times V\) (moles = concentration × volume) and \(V = \frac{n}{c}\) (volume = moles ÷ concentration). Volume must always be in dm³ when using mol/dm³ concentrations. To convert from cm³ to dm³, divide by 1000.

Key Fact

Concentration = moles ÷ volume (in dm³). To convert cm³ to dm³, divide by 1000. 250 cm³ = 0.250 dm³. Units of concentration: mol/dm³.

Titration Technique

Titration is the technique for measuring the volume of one solution needed to exactly react with a known volume of another. In an acid-alkali titration, the standard procedure (PAG C6) is:

A measured volume of alkali (using a pipette) is transferred to a conical flask. A few drops of indicator (such as phenolphthalein or methyl orange) are added. The acid is added from a burette, drop by drop near the end point, until the indicator changes colour permanently. This is the end point. The volume of acid used is read from the burette. The titration is repeated until two or more concordant results are obtained (usually within 0.10 cm³) and averaged.

25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution is placed in a conical flask. It requires 18.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid to reach the end point. The reaction is: \(\text{HCl} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\). Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide solution.

Step 1: Convert volumes to dm³. \(V_{\text{HCl}} = \frac{18.0}{1000} = 0.0180 \text{ dm}^3\) and \(V_{\text{NaOH}} = \frac{25.0}{1000} = 0.0250 \text{ dm}^3\).

Step 2: Calculate moles of HCl. \(n_{\text{HCl}} = c \times V = 0.200 \times 0.0180 = 0.00360 \text{ mol}\).

Step 3: Use the mole ratio. From the equation, 1 mol HCl reacts with 1 mol NaOH, so \(n_{\text{NaOH}} = 0.00360 \text{ mol}\).

Step 4: Calculate concentration of NaOH. \(c = \frac{n}{V} = \frac{0.00360}{0.0250} = 0.144 \text{ mol/dm}^3\).

Using Mole Ratios

The mole ratio from a balanced equation tells you how many moles of each substance react together. It is the key link between the solution whose concentration you know and the solution whose concentration you want to find.

For example, in the reaction of sulfuric acid with sodium hydroxide: \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\), the mole ratio is 1:2. If you calculate 0.0040 mol of H&sub2;SO&sub4; was used, then 0.0080 mol of NaOH reacted (double the moles of acid).

20.0 cm³ of sulfuric acid (H&sub2;SO&sub4;) reacts with 30.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide (NaOH). The equation is: \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\). Calculate the concentration of the sulfuric acid.

Step 1: Convert. \(V_{\text{NaOH}} = 0.0300 \text{ dm}^3\).

Step 2: Moles of NaOH. \(n_{\text{NaOH}} = 0.100 \times 0.0300 = 0.00300 \text{ mol}\).

Step 3: Mole ratio. 2 mol NaOH : 1 mol H&sub2;SO&sub4;, so \(n_{\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4} = \frac{0.00300}{2} = 0.00150 \text{ mol}\).

Step 4: Concentration. \(V_{\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4} = 0.0200 \text{ dm}^3\). \(c = \frac{0.00150}{0.0200} = 0.0750 \text{ mol/dm}^3\).

Key Fact

Titration calculation steps: (1) convert cm³ to dm³, (2) find moles of the known solution using \(n = c \times V\), (3) apply the mole ratio from the balanced equation, (4) find the unknown concentration using \(c = \frac{n}{V}\).

Common Errors to Avoid

In every titration calculation, the most frequent mistakes are: failing to convert cm³ to dm³ before calculating (this gives an answer 1000 times too large or too small); applying the wrong mole ratio (always check the balanced equation); and not stating units in the final answer. If you calculate moles of one substance and then forget to divide by the volume to get concentration, you have done two steps out of three correctly — always complete step 4.

Choosing the Right Indicator

The choice of indicator matters for getting a sharp, accurate end point. Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and turns pink in alkali — it is most useful when the alkali is in the burette and the acid is in the flask, because the colour change appears clearly in the flask at the end point. Methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in alkali, and is preferred for strong acid–weak base titrations where phenolphthalein gives a fuzzy end point. Universal indicator is never used in titrations because its gradual colour change makes it impossible to identify the precise end point. Whichever indicator you choose, add only two or three drops — excess indicator changes the pH of the solution and introduces error. Near the expected end point, add the titrant drop by drop and swirl the flask continuously; a single drop can take the solution past the end point if added too quickly. If you overshoot, the result must be discarded and the titration repeated.
exam_tip_html: Titration questions on the exam always reward method marks, so set out every step even if you make an arithmetic error. Use the layout: volume → dm³ (divide by 1000) → moles of known → moles of unknown (using mole ratio) → concentration. Never skip straight to a final answer. Check your mole ratio against the balanced equation — many errors come from assuming a 1:1 ratio without verifying. Include units throughout: mol for moles, dm³ for volume, mol/dm³ for concentration.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Concentration (mol/dm³) = moles ÷ volume (dm³). Always convert cm³ to dm³ by dividing by 1000 before substituting.
  • In a titration, a known volume of one solution is used to find the concentration of another. Repeat until concordant results (within 0.10 cm³) are obtained and average them.
  • The four-step method: convert volumes, find moles of the known solution, apply the mole ratio from the balanced equation, then calculate the unknown concentration.

practice_questions.text: Calculate the number of moles of solute in 250 cm³ of a 0.200 mol/dm³ sodium chloride solution.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Converts 250 cm³ to 0.250 dm³; applies n = c × V = 0.200 × 0.250 = 0.0500 mol; units stated.
Secure: Correct method with a minor arithmetic or unit error.
Developing: Sets up n = c × V but fails to convert cm³ to dm³, giving answer of 50 mol.
Emerging: Recalls the equation but cannot substitute or convert units.

practice_questions.text: Determine the concentration of a solution containing 0.0400 mol of potassium hydroxide dissolved in 500 cm³ of solution.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Converts 500 cm³ to 0.500 dm³; c = n ÷ V = 0.0400 ÷ 0.500 = 0.0800 mol/dm³; units correct.
Secure: Correct calculation with one minor error (e.g. rounding or unit omission).
Developing: Divides but uses 500 rather than 0.500, giving 0.0000800 mol/dm³.
Emerging: Equation recalled but not applied correctly.

practice_questions.text: In a titration, 25.0 cm³ of potassium hydroxide (KOH) solution requires 22.5 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid to reach the end point. The equation is: KOH + HCl → KCl + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the KOH solution.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: V(HCl) = 0.0225 dm³; n(HCl) = 0.100 × 0.0225 = 0.00225 mol; mole ratio 1:1 so n(KOH) = 0.00225 mol; V(KOH) = 0.0250 dm³; c(KOH) = 0.00225 ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0900 mol/dm³. Units throughout.
Secure: All steps shown, one arithmetic or conversion error.
Developing: Moles of HCl correct; ratio applied; final division step missing or incorrect.
Emerging: Concentration equation recalled but steps not completed.

practice_questions.text: A student carries out four titrations. Their results are: 18.40 cm³, 18.35 cm³, 17.80 cm³ and 18.30 cm³. Explain which results they should use to calculate the mean, and calculate the mean titre.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States that 17.80 cm³ is anomalous (more than 0.10 cm³ from the others) and should be excluded; mean of concordant results = (18.40 + 18.35 + 18.30) ÷ 3 = 18.35 cm³. Explanation of concordant results included.
Secure: Identifies anomalous result and calculates correct mean with minor rounding error.
Developing: Excludes anomalous result but does not explain why; mean calculation attempted.
Emerging: Some attempt to identify the outlier or calculate a mean, but not both.

practice_questions.text: Sulfuric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. 15.0 cm³ of 0.0500 mol/dm³ H₂SO₄ reacts completely with 25.0 cm³ of NaOH solution. Calculate the concentration of the NaOH solution.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: n(H₂SO₄) = 0.0500 × 0.0150 = 7.50 × 10⁻⁴ mol; mole ratio 1:2 so n(NaOH) = 1.50 × 10⁻³ mol; c(NaOH) = 1.50 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0600 mol/dm³; all units present.
Secure: Correct mole ratio applied; one arithmetic or conversion error.
Developing: Moles of acid calculated correctly; 1:2 ratio not applied (treats as 1:1).
Emerging: First step only — converts volume.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a student would carry out an accurate acid–alkali titration in the laboratory, including the steps taken to ensure a reliable result.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Describes using a pipette to measure a fixed volume of alkali into a conical flask; adding indicator (names one — e.g. phenolphthalein or methyl orange); filling burette with acid and noting initial reading; adding acid slowly, swirling the flask; adding drop by drop near the end point; noting the colour change at end point; recording final burette reading; calculating titre; repeating to obtain concordant results (within 0.10 cm³); calculating the mean of concordant titres. Clear, ordered description.
Secure: Most steps present; one or two missing (e.g. swirling or slow addition near end point).
Developing: Key apparatus named; end point identified; repeatability not mentioned.
Emerging: Some relevant apparatus named; partial procedure with significant omissions.

knowledge_checks.q: What are the units of molar concentration?
A student needs to convert 150 cm³ to dm³. What is the answer?
To find the number of moles in a solution, multiply the concentration by the _____ in dm³.
In a titration, you repeat the experiment until you obtain _____ results that agree within 0.10 cm³.
Match each term to its definition:
right: Technique to find volume of solution that reacts with a known volume of another
Point where indicator permanently changes colour
The ratio of moles of reactants from the balanced equation

flashcard_questions.q: What is the equation for molar concentration?
How do you convert 350 cm³ to dm³?
In a titration, what is the end point?
flashcard_questions.a: The point where the indicator permanently changes colour.
Results that agree within 0.10 cm³ and can be averaged reliably.

flashcard_questions.q: How many moles are in 100 cm³ of 0.500 mol/dm³ HCl?
The balanced equation is HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. What is the mole ratio of HCl to NaOH?
The balanced equation is H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. If 0.003 mol H₂SO₄ is used, how many moles of NaOH reacted?
What is the final step in a titration calculation?
flashcard_questions.a: Divide the moles of unknown by its volume (in dm³) to find its concentration.

flashcard_questions.q: Why must you convert cm³ to dm³ before using the concentration equation?
flashcard_questions.a: Concentration is in mol/dm³; using cm³ gives an answer 1000 times too large.

flashcard_questions.q: What indicator would change from pink to colourless at the end point of an alkali–acid titration?

glossary_terms.definition: The amount of solute (in moles) dissolved in one cubic decimetre (litre) of solution. Units: mol/dm³.
A practical technique used to find the volume of one solution that exactly reacts with a known volume of another solution, in order to determine an unknown concentration.
The point in a titration at which the indicator permanently changes colour, showing that the reaction is just complete.
Results that agree closely with one another, typically within 0.10 cm³ in titration, and can be averaged to give a reliable result.
The ratio of moles of reactants and products in a balanced chemical equation, given by the coefficients in front of each formula.
A long graduated tube with a tap, used in titrations to deliver precise measured volumes of a solution.
